title: Populations, gene pools and genetic variation — video support
purpose: Define a gene pool and distinguish change in a population from change within an individual.
fallback: Microevolution is a change in allele frequencies across generations. An allele frequency is its share of all allele copies at the locus. It is a proportion, not simply the number of individuals showing a trait. Suppose a population doubles in size while every allele’s proportion stays the same. The number of copies increases, but the allele frequencies have not changed. Conversely, frequencies can change even if the total population size remains constant. An individual’s body can grow, develop or adjust to conditions. Those changes are not themselves evidence that a population’s inherited allele frequencies have changed.

title: The Hardy–Weinberg model and its assumptions — video support
purpose: Explain the model’s conditions and distinguish allele totals from expected genotype frequencies.
fallback: The Hardy–Weinberg reference model assumes a very large population, random mating with respect to the locus, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection affecting the alleles or genotypes. A very large population minimizes chance fluctuations from sampling. Under these idealized conditions, allele frequencies remain constant across generations and genotype proportions follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The model gives a baseline for asking whether observed data fit the prediction. A real population need not satisfy every condition perfectly. A mismatch can suggest that assumptions need investigation, but the mismatch alone does not identify which mechanism caused it.

title: Calculating expected genotype frequencies — video support
purpose: Solve Hardy–Weinberg problems with explicit assumptions, separate quantities and reasonableness checks.
fallback: Use the allele frequencies to calculate the expected genotype frequencies: p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q² = 0.16. These are the expected fractions of AA, Aa and aa individuals. To obtain counts, multiply each frequency by N = 200. The expected numbers are 72 AA, 96 Aa and 32 aa. Check that the counts total 200 and the frequencies total 1. The heterozygotes are carriers in this simple recessive model. The dominant-phenotype fraction includes AA and Aa together, so it is 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, not p alone.

title: Natural selection and non-random mating — video support
purpose: Explain selection through differential reproductive success and distinguish it from mate-pairing effects.
fallback: A trait can increase survival but reduce mating opportunities, or increase mating success while imposing a survival cost. Sexual selection focuses on differences in obtaining mates and reproducing. For example, a conspicuous display might attract mates while also increasing exposure to predators. The overall evolutionary effect depends on the balance of reproductive consequences, not on whether the display appears efficient to an observer. A claim that selection occurred needs evidence relating heritable differences to reproductive outcomes. A change in frequency alone can also arise through chance or movement between populations.

title: Genetic drift, bottlenecks and founder effects — video support
purpose: Distinguish chance sampling from selection and compare bottleneck and founder cases.
fallback: A bottleneck occurs when population size falls sharply. The survivors may carry a smaller and unrepresentative sample of the earlier alleles. If the reduction is random with respect to a studied allele, drift can strongly change that allele’s frequency. If the population later increases, descendants reproduce the variation that survived. Recovery in numbers does not automatically bring back alleles that were lost. Mutation or gene flow might introduce variation later, but population growth alone does not guarantee restoration.

title: Genetic diversity and conservation evidence — video support
purpose: Use population-genetic mechanisms to evaluate conservation evidence without assuming a universal outcome.
fallback: A connection between habitats may permit movement and gene flow. If migrants reproduce, new alleles can enter a population and genetic differentiation may decline. Whether this happens depends on actual movement, survival and reproduction. A population-management proposal should specify its biological mechanism and the evidence needed to evaluate it. Adding individuals, improving habitat and connecting populations are different interventions with potentially different effects. The effects can include trade-offs. For example, introduced individuals may carry genetic variants suited to a different environment. An evidence-based evaluation considers both genetic contribution and the ecological setting rather than assuming that every transfer is beneficial.
